report:
## Report: Does opening a bedroom window or door improve sleep quality?

Your sister's claim is broadly supported by scientific evidence, though with important nuances.

**What the research shows**

A two-week field intervention study in 40 Danish bedrooms found that sleeping with an open window improved both objectively measured and subjectively rated sleep quality, and participants slept longer. Opening the bedroom door reduced CO₂ concentration but did not produce the same sleep benefits. The researchers noted that if ventilation keeps bedroom CO₂ below about 750 ppm, air quality is good enough that it no longer affects sleep (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605).

An earlier controlled study similarly showed that increasing ventilation—by opening a window or using quiet fans—reduced sleep onset latency, increased sleep efficiency, improved subjective sleep quality, and boosted next-day cognitive performance (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/).

A 2025 international literature review concluded that currently prescribed minimum residential ventilation rates may be too low for bedrooms and can lead to disturbed sleep, reinforcing that adequate ventilation matters (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/23744731.2025.2531317).

**Important caveats**

Benefits depend on conditions. Opening a window can let in outdoor noise, cold, heat, or pollutants (one study noted slightly higher NO₂ with windows open). Opening the door helps airflow but may not match window ventilation. The Sleep Foundation notes most people keep windows and doors closed despite the evidence (https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed).

**Bottom line:** Opening a window (more so than a door) tends to improve sleep quality by lowering CO₂ and improving indoor air quality, provided outdoor conditions are not disruptive.
